items.text: You can't trust Dr. Lee's research on nutrition — she's overweight herself.
items.explanation: Her weight has no bearing on whether the research is correct — ad hominem.

items.text: Why listen to his budget plan? He failed maths in high school.
items.explanation: Old grades don't refute the plan itself — ad hominem.

items.text: My coworker says we should recycle more, but he drives a gas-guzzler, so his point is nonsense.
items.explanation: His hypocrisy doesn't make the recycling point wrong — ad hominem.

items.text: Don't take her film review seriously — she never even went to film school.
items.explanation: Lacking a degree doesn't invalidate the review's reasoning — ad hominem.

items.text: His argument about saving water is worthless — he's rich and has a huge pool.
items.explanation: His lifestyle doesn't disprove the argument — ad hominem.

items.text: Everyone at my school uses this app, so it must be the best one.
items.explanation: Popularity says nothing about quality — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Millions of people follow this diet, so it has to work.
items.explanation: Lots of believers doesn't make it effective — appeal to popularity.

items.text: This song is number one on the charts, so it's obviously the greatest song of the year.
items.explanation: Chart position reflects sales, not quality — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Most of my friends want to skip class, so it's clearly the right thing to do.
items.explanation: Friends agreeing doesn't make it right — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Everybody's putting money into this coin, so it can't be a bad investment.
items.explanation: Widespread hype isn't proof of a good investment — appeal to popularity.

items.text: Either we cancel the whole trip or we go completely bankrupt — there's no other choice.
items.explanation: There are options besides those two extremes — false dilemma.

items.text: You're either with us on this decision or you're against the whole team.
items.explanation: Disagreeing on one thing doesn't make you an enemy — false dilemma.

items.text: If we don't buy the newest phone, we'll be completely left behind in life.
items.explanation: Not upgrading isn't the same as being left behind — false dilemma.

items.text: We either ban screens for kids entirely or accept that they'll fail school.
items.explanation: There's plenty of middle ground between the two — false dilemma.

items.text: Either you finish the entire marathon today or you're not a real runner.
items.explanation: Runners exist between those two extremes — false dilemma.

items.text: The two Italian restaurants I tried were bad, so Italian food is just overrated.
items.explanation: Two meals can't judge a whole cuisine — hasty generalization.

items.text: My uncle smoked his whole life and lived to 90, so smoking clearly isn't harmful.
items.explanation: One case can't overturn the overall evidence — hasty generalization.

items.text: I met two rude tourists from that country, so people there must all be rude.
items.explanation: Two people don't represent a whole country — hasty generalization.

items.text: This brand's laptop broke on me once, so all their products are junk.
items.explanation: One failure isn't the whole product line — hasty generalization.

items.text: Both people I asked prefer tea, so basically everyone prefers tea over coffee.
items.explanation: Two people can't speak for everyone — hasty generalization.

items.text: A famous actor endorsed this supplement, so it must genuinely boost your memory.
items.explanation: An actor isn't a medical expert — appeal to authority.

items.text: My favorite streamer said this stock will moon, so it's a guaranteed win.
items.explanation: A streamer isn't a financial expert — appeal to authority.

items.text: A Nobel-winning physicist said this diet works, so it must be right.
items.explanation: Expertise in physics doesn't transfer to nutrition — appeal to authority.

items.text: The CEO said the product is perfectly safe, so there's no need to check any reviews.
items.explanation: The seller's own word isn't independent proof — appeal to authority.

items.text: A celebrity chef swears by this pan, so it has to be the best cookware for everyone.
items.explanation: One chef's endorsement isn't proof it's best for you — appeal to authority.

items.text: Every player on the team is over six feet tall. Sam is on the team. So Sam is over six feet tall.
items.explanation: The conclusion follows necessarily from the premises — it's valid.

items.text: If it rains, the match is cancelled. It's raining. So the match is cancelled.
items.explanation: A textbook valid step (modus ponens) — nothing is wrong.

items.text: Every book on this shelf is nonfiction. This book is on the shelf. Therefore this book is nonfiction.
items.explanation: The conclusion is guaranteed by the premises — valid.

items.text: The store is closed every Sunday. Today is Sunday. So the store is closed today.
items.explanation: The conclusion follows directly from the premises — valid.

items.text: She saves $200 every month. That's $2,400 over twelve months. So in a year she'll have saved $2,400.
items.explanation: The arithmetic follows from the premise — valid.
